title: Build the Opening Three Songs

sections.title: Shape the set
sections.description: Rank, match and slide your way through the opener.

sections.title: Four first-song promises
sections.description: Pick the promise you'd rather make.

dimensions.description: Whether you prefer a set to earn attention gradually or grab it from the first moment.
Whether you prefer songs to flow into each other or to change the mood with a jolt.

questions.prompt: Your room is half-full and nervous. Rank these opener mood cards from most to least like what you'd play first.
questions.context: Cards describe moods only, with no song titles. There are no right answers; your order shapes your result.
questions.explanation: Cards that grow gradually point toward a Slow Build, while instant payoffs point toward an Immediate Hook. A hush that suddenly gives way to impact leans toward Sharp Contrasts.

items.label: A low pulse that swells gradually over two minutes
A big shared refrain from the very first beat
One quiet voice for a minute, then the full band crashes in
A sudden loud burst right after silence

questions.context: Several situations can share the same approach. Choose what feels natural for you.
questions.explanation: Your choices show whether you adapt by building slowly or hooking quickly, and whether you connect songs smoothly or switch moods abruptly.

right.label: Let one idea grow slowly into the next
Lead with the strongest hook, then cut to something new
Lead with a hook, then glide into a similar feel
Start gently, then drop a sudden contrast

questions.prompt: How long should the first song wait before delivering its biggest moment?
questions.context: Slide toward the left for a long wait and toward the right for an instant payoff.
questions.explanation: A long wait suggests you like tension to accumulate. A near-instant payoff suggests you want listeners hooked immediately.
questions.highLabel: Hook in the first ten seconds

questions.prompt: Rank these ways of moving from song one to song two, from most to least appealing.
questions.context: All four are described by feel only. There is no correct order.
questions.explanation: Steady or overlapping transitions favor Smooth Transitions. Stops and drastic volume swings favor Sharp Contrasts.

items.label: Keep the tempo and overall feel steady
Overlap the ending with a shared texture
Stop dead, then begin something quite different
Jump from loud to nearly silent

questions.prompt: Which first-song promise feels stronger to you?
questions.explanation: Rewarding patience points to a Slow Build, while instant recognition points to an Immediate Hook.

options.label: Stay with me, and the payoff will be worth it
You'll know exactly why you're here right away

questions.prompt: Which promise about the whole set sounds better to you?
questions.explanation: Flow-first promises favor Smooth Transitions. Surprise-first promises favor Sharp Contrasts.

options.label: Every song will lead naturally into the next
Every song will change the mood on you

questions.prompt: Which first minute would you rather design?
questions.explanation: Withholding the main melody is a Slow Build tactic. Presenting it immediately is an Immediate Hook tactic.

options.label: Hint at the main melody but hold it back
Play the main melody in the first bar

questions.prompt: Which pairing of the first two mood cards would you rather use?
questions.explanation: A pairing that shifts energy sharply favors Sharp Contrasts. A pairing at a similar energy level favors Smooth Transitions.

A medium card followed by a similar medium card

title: Festival Route Planner

sections.title: Build the day
sections.description: Order stops and check walking gaps.

sections.title: Repair the route

questions.prompt: Put the four acts in the order you will see them, using every clue.
questions.context: Clues: Acts A and D both play North Stage, and A is earlier. Act B plays Lantern Tent and happens between A and D. Act C plays Riverside Deck and is the finale.
questions.explanation: A comes before B, B before D, and C closes the day, so the only valid order is A, B, D, C.

questions.prompt: Order the five parts of the afternoon, including your friend's nap, so every clue holds.
questions.context: Clues: Act G opens the day. Act E comes after G. The nap is the only break and sits between Act E and Act F. Act H closes the day.
questions.explanation: G opens and H closes. The nap sits between E and F, so the middle runs E, nap, F, giving G, E, Nap, F, H.

questions.prompt: What is the latest minute you can leave North Stage and still reach Lantern Tent by 6:30 pm?
questions.context: Invented festival. Walking from North Stage to Lantern Tent takes 20 minutes. Act B starts at 6:40 pm, and you want a 10-minute cushion to find a spot.
questions.explanation: To arrive by 6:30 pm with a 20-minute walk, subtract 20 minutes from 6:30. The latest departure is 6:10 pm.

questions.prompt: Act D runs 7:00 pm at Riverside Deck. Decide whether each earlier set leaves you enough time to reach it.
questions.context: Invented data. Walks: Lantern Tent to Riverside Deck is 20 minutes; North Stage to Riverside Deck is 5 minutes; a set already at Riverside Deck needs no walk. Act D starts at 7:00 pm and you must arrive by then.
questions.explanation: Lantern sets need a 20-minute walk, so a 6:55 finish arrives at 7:15 and a set ending at 7:10 overlaps D. A North Stage finish at 6:40 arrives at 6:45, and a Riverside set ending at 6:50 needs no walk.

questions.prompt: Walking straight from Act B to Act D makes you late. Which change lets you see all of both?
questions.context: Invented festival. Act B ends 6:40 pm at Lantern Tent. Act D plays Riverside Deck 6:50–7:30 pm, with a repeat at Garden Stage 7:10–7:50 pm. Walks from Lantern: Riverside 20 min, Garden 15 min, North Stage 5 min. North Stage to Riverside is 10 min.
questions.explanation: Garden Stage is a 15-minute walk, so you arrive at 6:55 for the 7:10 repeat. Every other option is late or misses part of Act B.

options.label: Walk to Garden Stage for the repeat set
Leave Act B ten minutes early for Riverside Deck
Detour through North Stage, then go to Riverside Deck

questions.prompt: Two sets overlap. You must keep Act B and Act D. Which set should you drop?
questions.context: Invented schedule. Act A: North Stage 4:00–4:45 pm. Act B: Lantern Tent 5:00–5:45. Act C: Lantern Tent 5:30–6:15. Act D: Riverside Deck 6:20–7:00. North Stage to Lantern is 10 minutes; Lantern to Riverside is 20.
questions.explanation: Act C overlaps Act B, so it has to go. Act A still reaches B in time, and B reaches D at 6:05, before 6:20.

questions.prompt: Label each planned hop by whether you arrive early, exactly on time, or late.
questions.context: Invented plan, all times pm. Hop 1: leave 3:10, walk 20, set starts 3:30. Hop 2: leave 4:05, walk 15, set starts 4:30. Hop 3: leave 5:10, walk 20, set starts 5:25. Hop 4: leave 6:00, walk 20, set starts 6:20.
questions.explanation: Add each walk to its departure: 3:30 and 6:20 are exact, 4:20 is ten minutes early, and 5:30 is five minutes late.

questions.prompt: The plan has you at Act B's 7:50 pm set. Which repair fixes that and still shows all of Act D?
questions.context: Invented rules: see all of Act B before sunset (7:45 pm) and all of Act D. Act B plays Lantern Tent 5:20–6:00 pm and 7:50–8:30 pm. Act D plays Riverside Deck 6:25–7:05 pm. Lantern to Riverside is 20 minutes.
questions.explanation: Seeing B's early set ends at 6:00, so you reach D at 6:20 for its 6:25 start. The later B set is after sunset, and leaving early misses part of B.

options.label: See Act B's 5:20 set fully, then walk to Act D
Stay with the 7:50 set of Act B
Leave Act B's early set at 5:50 for Act D
Watch Act D first, then Act B's 7:50 set

title: Behind the Album Credits
description: Read invented liner notes, match credit lines to typical jobs, order a recording workflow, and decide who to ask when a fictional album hits a problem.

questions.prompt: Match each credit line from the invented album Lantern Tide to the job it typically describes.
questions.context: Roles vary by project, but these are typical meanings in this quiz.

right.label: Composing the song's melody and words
Guiding the creative direction of the sessions
Balancing recorded tracks into one finished song
Preparing the finished songs for consistent album playback

questions.explanation: Writers create the song, producers steer the sessions, mixers balance tracks inside a song, and mastering engineers prepare the final songs to play consistently together.

questions.prompt: On the invented album Harbor Static, match each credit to what that person typically did.

right.label: Captured the performances with microphones and equipment
Performed an instrument part on the recording
Set the loudness of the whole album for release

questions.explanation: Tracking and recording credits both point to capturing sound, while an instrument credit names a performer. Lyrics and album loudness are other jobs.

questions.prompt: A liner note says: 'Arranged by Noor Haddad: wrote the horn parts each player reads on Salt Road.' Which role is credited?
questions.explanation: An arranger typically decides how parts are voiced and written for players. Here Noor wrote horn parts, not lyrics, sound capture, or final album preparation.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for one song on an invented album, from earliest to latest.
questions.context: Assume a song is written first, then recorded, then mixed, and only then mastered with the other songs.
questions.explanation: There must be a song before it is recorded, recorded tracks before mixing, and a finished mix before it is mastered for the album.

questions.prompt: On the invented song Paper Moons, the vocal is buried under guitars, though the recordings are clean. Who do you ask?
questions.context: Only this song has the problem. The other songs sound balanced, and the album plays consistently.
questions.explanation: Balance among tracks inside one song is a typical mixing task. The mastering engineer works on finished songs as a set.

questions.prompt: A hum appears on a guitar track from the live room. You need to know which cables and microphones were used. Who do you ask?
questions.explanation: The recording engineer typically knows the session setup, such as microphone choices, placement, and signal path, that produced the captured sound.

questions.prompt: Before another vocal session, the singer wants the second verse's words rewritten. Whose input is typically needed?
questions.explanation: Changing the words means changing the composition, which is typically the songwriter's work, not capturing, balancing, or preparing recordings.

questions.prompt: For each problem on an invented album, choose the role you would typically contact first.

cells.label: Two full takes exist, and someone must choose one and shape tomorrow's session plan
Twelve finished songs jump noticeably in loudness when played in sequence
The bridge needs entirely new words

questions.explanation: Producers guide session decisions, mastering engineers handle consistency across finished songs, and songwriters create words and melody.

title: Sample or Cover? Concepts Edition
description: Sort invented music scenarios into sample, cover, interpolation, remix or tribute using the quiz's own definitions, then pick the detail that settles two tricky edge cases.

questions.prompt: A musician re-records a familiar melody inside a new song with new lyrics. Which label fits best?
questions.context: Quiz definitions: Sample = reuses actual audio from an existing recording. Cover = new performance of an existing song, kept largely intact. Interpolation = re-performs part of an existing melody or lyric inside a new song. Remix = rebuilds an existing recording from its own parts. Tribute = original work honoring someone, borrowing nothing.
questions.explanation: The melody is newly performed, not lifted audio, and it sits inside a different song. That matches interpolation rather than a cover of the whole song.

questions.prompt: Producer Amara copies two seconds of drums straight from an old record's audio file and loops them under her new beat. Which label fits?
questions.context: Quiz definitions: Sample = reuses actual audio from an existing recording. Cover = new performance of an existing song. Interpolation = re-performs part of an existing melody inside a new song. Remix = rebuilds a recording from its own parts. Tribute = original work borrowing nothing.
questions.explanation: Amara takes real audio from an existing recording and places it in a new track. That is the defining feature of sampling.

questions.prompt: Composer Leila writes a brand-new instrumental that salutes her late mentor's style, using none of the mentor's melodies, words or recordings. Which label fits?
questions.context: Quiz definitions: Sample = reuses actual audio. Cover = new performance of an existing song. Interpolation = re-performs part of an existing melody or lyric. Remix = rebuilds a recording from its own parts. Tribute = original work honoring someone, borrowing nothing.
questions.explanation: Nothing is reused or re-performed. The piece only honors a style and a person, which fits the tribute definition.

questions.prompt: Match each invented scenario to the label that fits it best. Some labels can be used more than once.
questions.context: Quiz definitions: Cover = new performance of an existing song, largely intact. Remix = rebuilds an existing recording from its own parts, possibly adding layers. Tribute = original work honoring someone, borrowing nothing. Sample and interpolation are also available.

left.label: DJ Pilar rearranges the vocal, bass and drum tracks of an existing release into a longer club version.
A choir records a whole existing song in its own harmonies, keeping the melody and words.
DJ Wen keeps an existing release's vocal track, mutes its guitar track and adds a synth bed of her own.

questions.explanation: Pilar and Wen both rebuild an existing recording from its own parts, so both are remixes. The choir newly performs a whole song, which is a cover.

questions.prompt: Pick the best label for each invented studio situation.
questions.context: Quiz definitions: Sample = actual audio lifted from a recording. Cover = new performance of a whole existing song. Interpolation = re-performs part of an existing melody or lyric in a new song. Remix = rebuilds a recording from its own parts.

cells.label: Koji cuts a one-second vocal shout from an old release's file and pitches it into his hook.
Mei sings a complete existing song in a different language, keeping its tune and meaning.
Ola plays a short brass riff from an existing song on her own keyboard, then builds a new tune around it.

questions.explanation: Koji uses real audio, Mei performs a whole song anew, and Ola re-plays only a fragment inside a new song. Those are sample, cover and interpolation respectively.

questions.prompt: A pianist plays her own new piece but, midway, replays eight recognizable notes of an existing melody herself. Which label fits?
questions.context: Quiz definitions: Sample = reuses actual audio. Cover = new performance of an existing song, kept largely intact. Interpolation = re-performs part of an existing melody inside a new work. Remix = rebuilds a recording from its own parts. Tribute = borrows nothing.
questions.explanation: Only a fragment is borrowed, it is newly performed, and the surrounding piece is original. That is interpolation, not a cover or a sample.

questions.prompt: Rhea's track repeats a one-bar hook that matches an old song's melody. Which detail best separates a sample from an interpolation?
questions.context: Edge case: both labels involve borrowed musical material, so the deciding detail is how the sound was produced.

options.label: Whether the audio came from the old recording or was newly performed
Whether the track tempo is fast
Whether the new title is shorter

questions.explanation: A sample reuses the original audio itself. An interpolation re-performs the melody or lyric. Catchiness, tempo and title length do not distinguish them.

questions.prompt: Two versions of an existing song circulate. Which detail best separates a cover from a remix?
questions.context: Edge case: both versions keep the song recognizable. Industry usage of these terms can overlap, so this quiz uses its own definitions. This is general education, not legal advice.

options.label: Whether the version is longer than the original
Whether it is newly performed or rebuilt from the original recording's parts

questions.explanation: A cover is a fresh performance of the song. A remix reworks the original recording's own parts. Recognizability, length and fame can apply to both.

title: Instrument, Sound, Role Links
description: Match invented ensemble instruments to how they make sound, link described sound patterns to band roles, then connect several instruments to one shared role.

sections.title: How the sound starts
sections.description: Classify instruments by their sound production.

sections.title: Sounds to roles
sections.description: Link sound patterns to the job they do.

sections.title: Many to one
sections.description: Connect different instruments to a shared role.

questions.prompt: For the invented Harbor Lantern Ensemble, match each instrument to the way its sound is produced.
questions.context: Rule: classify by the part that keeps ringing and carries the tone. Thrumbox: player plucks taut cords over a wooden box. Gourdhorn: player buzzes lips into a long curved tube. Tapslab: player hits wooden bars with mallets. Glowtone: a circuit makes an electrical wave sent to a speaker.
questions.explanation: Each instrument's tone comes from a different ringing part: cords, buzzing lips with a tube, wooden bars, or a circuit-made wave.

questions.prompt: Echo-Keys has keys that swing felt hammers onto taut metal cords, and the cords ring on. Which production type fits?
questions.context: Same rule as before: classify by the part that keeps ringing and carries the tone, not by the part that starts the contact. Echo-Keys is an invented instrument.
questions.explanation: The hammer only starts the sound. The metal cords keep ringing and carry the tone, so the rule places Echo-Keys with vibrating cords.

questions.prompt: Which two invented instruments share the same sound-production type?
questions.context: Bowlyre: a rosined bow rubs its cords. Plucktar: fingers pluck its cords. Buzzhorn: the player's lips buzz in a tube. Padbox: a circuit generates a wave for a speaker.
questions.explanation: Bowing and plucking are different playing actions, but in both cases vibrating cords carry the tone. The other pairs mix different sound sources.

questions.prompt: Match each described sound pattern to the ensemble role it is playing in this invented arrangement.
questions.context: Role legend: Foundation is a deep note anchoring each bar. Pulse is even taps on the beats. Lead is the main tune. Sparkle is brief high decoration between phrases. Roles are often assigned this way, though arrangements vary.

left.label: One deep note at the start of each four-beat bar
Equal soft taps on all four beats
A long singable tune moving through several pitches
Three tiny high pings in the pause after a phrase

questions.explanation: Each pattern matches its legend entry: bar-level deep notes anchor, beat taps mark pulse, the tune leads, and short high pings decorate.

questions.prompt: A part plays one deep note at each bar start. At 500 ms per beat in four-beat bars, what is its role and note spacing?
questions.context: Legend: Foundation is one deep note per bar. Pulse is a tap on every beat. Beat length is 500 ms and each bar has 4 beats. This tempo is an invented setting.
questions.explanation: A bar lasts 4 × 500 = 2000 ms, so one note per bar is spaced 2000 ms apart. One deep note per bar is the Foundation job.

questions.prompt: In Song 1 the Thrumbox plays Foundation, but in Song 2 it plays the Lead tune. What does this support?
questions.context: The Thrumbox is an invented instrument, and both songs are invented arrangements for the same ensemble.

options.label: A role describes a part in one arrangement, so instruments can switch roles
The Thrumbox must have been classified wrongly in one song
Changing roles changes how the instrument makes sound
Each role can be played by only one instrument

questions.explanation: Roles belong to the parts in an arrangement. The Thrumbox still makes sound with cords in both songs, so roles are often typical, not fixed.

questions.prompt: In the invented Tide Song arrangement, link each instrument's part to the role it fills. Several can share a role.
questions.context: Parts: Thrumbox plays one deep note per bar. Gourdhorn plays one deep note per bar. Glowtone bass patch plays one deep note per bar. Tapslab taps every beat. Reedpipe plays the main tune. Roles: Foundation, Pulse, Lead.
questions.explanation: Three different instruments, with three different sound sources, can all fill Foundation. The beat-tapping part is Pulse and the tune part is Lead.

questions.prompt: In the invented Moon Bridge arrangement, three instruments share the Foundation role. Choose each one's sound-production type.
questions.context: Strumbass: heavy cords plucked by fingers. Lowhorn: lips buzz in a coiled tube. Boomsynth: a circuit makes a low electrical wave for a speaker. All three play one deep note per bar.
questions.explanation: One shared role can be filled by three different sound sources: plucked cords, buzzing lips in a tube, and a circuit-made wave.

title: Genre Family Tree Builder
description: Work through invented music styles: match styles to families, link blended styles to every family they qualify for, trace shared roots, and order emergence from clues.

sections.title: Families
sections.description: Sort styles into families and check tempo.

sections.title: Blends and roots
sections.description: Link styles to every parent and root.

sections.title: Timelines
sections.description: Order styles from clues.

questions.prompt: Match each invented style to the family whose defining traits it shows.
questions.context: Every style, family and trait here is invented for this quiz. Pulses are counted in a bar; a big pulse can be split into three smaller ones.

left.label: Saltwind: six counts, big pulses on 1 and 4, rolling hand drums
Brightrail: four steady pulses, fast, sharp accents on 2 and 4
Hushbell: chords held eight pulses, no drums, very slow
Foamstep: six counts, big pulses on 1 and 4, rolling drums, quicker than Saltwind

right.label: Tide family: two big pulses each split in three, rolling hand drums
Spark family: four fast pulses with accents on 2 and 4
Lantern family: very slow, long held chords, almost no drums

questions.explanation: Saltwind and Foamstep both group six counts as two big pulses of three, so they share the Tide family. Brightrail is Spark and Hushbell is Lantern.

questions.prompt: Under the two-of-three rule, which family does the style Cobaltwave join?
questions.context: Rule: a style joins a family when it shows at least two of that family's three traits. Tide: compound six-count grouping, rolling hand drums, call-and-response chants. Spark: fast four-pulse, backbeat accents, shouted hooks. Lantern: very slow tempo, held chords, sparse drums. Cobaltwave has fast four-pulse, backbeat accents and rolling hand drums.

options.label: No family, since it has traits from two

questions.explanation: Cobaltwave shows two Spark traits (fast four-pulse and backbeat accents) but only one Tide trait, so Spark is the only family it joins.

questions.prompt: Which style's pulse length puts it in the Spark tempo range?
questions.context: Pulses per minute = 60,000 ÷ milliseconds per pulse. A style counts as Spark-tempo when it runs 140 to 180 pulses per minute. Each option gives the length of one pulse.
questions.explanation: 60,000 ÷ 400 = 150 pulses per minute, inside the range. Ashrun runs 200, Dewfall 100 and Mistdrift (1,200 ms) 50.

questions.prompt: Which pair of families shares the root Pulsewood?
questions.context: In this invented tree, the root Pulsewood has two child families: Tide and Spark. A separate root, Stillwood, has one child family: Lantern. The two roots are unrelated.
questions.explanation: Only Tide and Spark sit under Pulsewood. Lantern descends from Stillwood, and the two roots do not share an ancestor.

questions.prompt: Link each blended style to every family it qualifies for under the two-of-three rule.
questions.context: Rule: link a style to a family if it shows at least two of that family's three traits. Tide: compound grouping, rolling hand drums, call-and-response chants. Spark: fast four-pulse, backbeat accents, shouted hooks. Lantern: very slow tempo, held chords, sparse drums. Glowtide: compound grouping, rolling hand drums, held chords, very slow tempo. Dashfoam: rolling hand drums, call-and-response chants, backbeat accents, shouted hooks. Cinderpad: sparse drums, held chords, backbeat accents.
questions.explanation: Glowtide qualifies for Tide and Lantern, Dashfoam for Tide and Spark. Cinderpad has only one Spark trait, so it links to Lantern alone.

questions.prompt: Link each style to every root it descends from, following its parent families.
questions.context: Pulsewood is the root of Tide and Spark. Stillwood is the root of Lantern. Parent families: Glowtide has Tide and Lantern; Dashfoam has Tide and Spark; Cinderpad has Lantern; Moonreel has Spark and Lantern.
questions.explanation: A style descends from a root through each parent. Glowtide and Moonreel have parents under both roots, Dashfoam only Pulsewood, and Cinderpad only Stillwood.

questions.prompt: Order these styles from earliest to latest using the clues; some may tie.
questions.context: Invented timeline clues: Saltwind is the oldest of the four. Foamstep grew out of Saltwind. Glowtide also grew out of Saltwind. Dashfoam needed both Foamstep and Glowtide to exist first. Nothing says which of Foamstep or Glowtide came first.
questions.explanation: Saltwind comes first and Dashfoam last. Foamstep and Glowtide both fit in the middle in either order because the clues do not rank them.

questions.prompt: Put these styles in the order they emerged, earliest first.
questions.context: Invented timeline clues: Brightrail formed in reaction to Hushbell. Cobaltwave borrowed Brightrail's accents. Cinderpad copied Cobaltwave's rolling drums, so it appeared after Cobaltwave.
questions.explanation: Each clue links neighbors in a chain: Hushbell, then Brightrail, then Cobaltwave, then Cinderpad. Only that one order satisfies all three clues.

title: Music Terms Without the Panic
description: Match everyday scenes to terms like crescendo, staccato and legato, then put dynamics and tempo words in order, using a short legend on each task.

sections.title: Everyday scenes
sections.description: Pick the term that fits.

sections.title: Match and decode
sections.description: Link scenes to terms.

sections.title: Put in order
sections.description: Sort by loudness and speed.

questions.prompt: A storyteller's voice rises little by little as footsteps near the door. Which term describes that change?
questions.context: Legend: crescendo = gradually getting louder. Diminuendo = gradually getting softer. Staccato = short, detached notes. Legato = smooth, connected notes.
questions.explanation: A gradual rise in volume is a crescendo. The other terms describe getting softer or how separate or connected notes sound, not a change in loudness.

questions.prompt: Someone crosses a creaky floor with quick, separate taps and tiny silences between each one. Which term fits the style?
questions.context: Legend: crescendo = gradually louder. Staccato = short, detached notes. Legato = smooth, connected notes. Fermata = hold a note longer than written.
questions.explanation: Short notes with gaps between them are staccato. Legato is the opposite, and fermata and crescendo concern held length and volume change instead.

questions.prompt: A hand glides along a banister without lifting off, like notes flowing into one another. Which term matches?
questions.context: Legend: legato = smooth, connected notes. Staccato = short, detached notes. Diminuendo = gradually softer. Accelerando = gradually faster.
questions.explanation: Smooth, unbroken connection between notes is legato. Nothing in the banister scene gets softer or faster, so the other terms do not apply.

questions.prompt: A wind-up toy ticks at the same volume, but each tick comes a little later than the last. Which term fits?
questions.context: Legend: ritardando = gradually slower. Accelerando = gradually faster. Diminuendo = gradually softer. Fermata = hold a note longer than written. Tempo means speed of the beat.
questions.explanation: The beat is gradually slowing while volume stays level, so it is a ritardando. Diminuendo would need the ticks to get quieter.

questions.prompt: Match each scene to the term that describes its change. Some terms can be used more than once.
questions.context: Legend: crescendo = gradually louder. Diminuendo = gradually softer. Ritardando = gradually slower beat.

left.label: Rain begins as a whisper and ends as a roaring downpour
A music box plays quieter with each turn of the crank
A crowd claps harder and harder until the room shakes
A rolling cart's rattling beat spaces out until it stops

questions.explanation: Growing louder is crescendo, used for the rain and the clapping. Growing softer is diminuendo. A beat spacing out is ritardando, which is about speed, not volume.

questions.prompt: Choose the term for each situation. Each cell has one best answer.
questions.context: Legend: fermata = hold longer than written. Accelerando = gradually faster. Diminuendo = gradually softer. Legato = smooth and connected.

cells.label: A singer lets the last note of a lullaby hang longer than its written length
During a chase scene, the drum beat gets steadily quicker
The final bars of a song fade, each quieter than the one before

questions.explanation: A held note is a fermata, a quickening beat is accelerando, and a fade to softness is diminuendo. Each term names one separate idea: length, speed or volume.

questions.prompt: Order these loudness marks from quietest to loudest.
questions.context: Legend: pianissimo = very soft. Piano = soft. Forte = loud. Fortissimo = very loud.
questions.explanation: Pianissimo is softest, then piano, then forte, with fortissimo loudest. The double ending intensifies the base word in each pair.

questions.prompt: Order these tempo words from slowest to fastest.
questions.context: Legend: largo = very slow. Andante = an easy walking pace. Allegro = quick and lively. Presto = very fast. Conventions vary slightly between musicians.
questions.explanation: Largo is slowest, andante is a walking pace, allegro is brisk and presto is fastest. Tempo words describe speed, so they are separate from loudness words.

title: Studio Trick Translator
description: Use a short studio cheat card to match what you hear described to reverb, compression, panning, or pitch correction, then pick the right fix for four mixing problems.

questions.prompt: A vocal's last word keeps ringing for three seconds, as if sung in a stone hall. Which tool made that?
questions.context: Studio card: Reverb adds a fading tail of room reflections. Compression narrows the loudness gap between soft and loud moments. Panning places a sound between the left and right speakers. Pitch correction nudges sung notes toward a chosen scale.
questions.explanation: A lingering, fading tail after the sound stops is what reverb adds. The other tools change loudness range, left-right position, or note pitch, not room echo.

questions.prompt: A shaker starts only in your left earbud, then glides to your right earbud over four bars. What was automated?
questions.context: Studio card: Reverb adds a fading tail of room reflections. Compression narrows the loudness gap between soft and loud moments. Panning places a sound between the left and right speakers. Pitch correction nudges sung notes toward a chosen scale.
questions.explanation: Moving a sound's position from left to right across the stereo field is panning. Nothing about its tail, loudness range, or pitch needs to change.

questions.prompt: Match each description to the studio technique most directly responsible. Some techniques are used more than once.
questions.context: Studio card: Reverb adds a fading tail of room reflections. Compression narrows the loudness gap between soft and loud moments. Panning places a sound between the left and right speakers. Pitch correction nudges sung notes toward a chosen scale.
questions.explanation: Match each effect to the one thing the tool changes: tail, loudness range, stereo position, or pitch. Two descriptions are about loudness range, so both are compression.

left.label: Whispered words now sit at nearly the same loudness as shouted ones
A slightly flat sung note now lands on its scale note
A clap seems to ring on in an empty tunnel after it stops
Backing vocals sit far left while the lead stays in the center
A podcast voice no longer jumps loud on sudden laughs

questions.prompt: Each knob was turned up. Pick the audible change you would expect from each one.
questions.context: Studio card: Reverb adds a fading tail of room reflections. Compression narrows the loudness gap between soft and loud moments. Panning places a sound between the left and right speakers. Pitch correction nudges sung notes toward a chosen scale.
questions.explanation: Each knob changes only its own property: tail length for reverb decay, loudness gap for compression ratio, position for pan, and note snapping for correction strength.

cells.label: Reverb decay raised from 0.5 to 3 seconds

options.label: Sound moves toward the right speaker
Notes snap harder to the scale

cells.label: Compression ratio raised from gentle to firm

options.label: Sound moves toward the right speaker
Notes snap harder to the scale

cells.label: Pan knob moved from center to 70% right

options.label: Sound moves toward the right speaker
Notes snap harder to the scale

cells.label: Correction strength raised from gentle to full

options.label: Sound moves toward the right speaker
Notes snap harder to the scale

questions.prompt: In a busy chorus, each syllable blurs into the next. Which fix keeps some room feel but clears the words?
questions.context: The vocal has a 4-second reverb tail. Goal: keep a little room sound, but make the lyrics clear. Studio card: reverb adds a fading tail of room reflections.
questions.explanation: The blur comes from a very long tail overlapping the next syllables. Shortening the decay keeps some space while letting each word land clearly.

options.label: Raise pitch correction to full strength
Shorten the reverb decay to about 1 second

questions.prompt: Quiet verse lines vanish under the drums, while loud chorus lines are fine. Which change best evens out the vocal?
questions.context: The singer's level swings widely within each line. Goal: even out only the vocal's loudness without turning down the drums. Studio card: compression narrows the loudness gap between soft and loud moments.
questions.explanation: The problem is a wide gap between soft and loud vocal moments, which is what compression narrows. Reverb, panning, and pitch fixes do not change loudness range.

options.label: Apply pitch correction to the whole take

questions.prompt: Two guitar parts, both centered, mask each other. Which fix separates them without changing volume or tone?
questions.context: Both guitars have the same loudness and tone and sit in the exact center. Goal: let listeners tell them apart. Studio card: panning places a sound between the left and right speakers.
questions.explanation: Sending one guitar left and the other right gives each its own space in the stereo field. Compression, reverb, and pitch correction would not separate their positions.

options.label: Add the same reverb to both guitars
Apply pitch correction to both guitars
Pan one guitar left and the other right

questions.prompt: One held note at the song's end is slightly under pitch, and the rest is fine. Which fix targets just that?
questions.context: Goal: bring that single note to its intended scale pitch while leaving the other notes alone. Studio card: pitch correction nudges sung notes toward a chosen scale.
questions.explanation: Pitch correction applied to that one note moves it toward the scale pitch. Reverb, panning, and compression leave the pitch exactly where it was.

options.label: Pan the whole vocal to the center
Apply gentle pitch correction to that note
Lengthen the reverb on the whole vocal
Raise the compression ratio on the whole vocal

title: Rehearsal Cue Chain
description: Order fictional band entrances from beat and millisecond cue rules, then pick the single cue change that fixes a timing conflict.

sections.title: Cue chains
sections.description: Rebuild who enters when.

sections.title: Cue repairs
sections.description: Fix the timing conflict.

questions.prompt: Order these four entrances from earliest to latest using the rehearsal rules.
questions.context: Beats are numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on. Drums hit on beats 1, 2, 3 and 4. Bass enters on the beat right after the second drum hit. Keys enter one beat before bass. Tambourine enters one beat after bass. Guitar enters two beats after bass.
questions.explanation: The second drum hit is beat 2, so bass is beat 3. Keys are beat 2, tambourine beat 4, and guitar beat 5.

questions.prompt: Order the four entrances from earliest to latest in this four-beat-bar rehearsal.
questions.context: Every bar has 4 beats, and beat counting continues across bars: bar 2 holds beats 5 to 8. Drums enter on beat 2 of bar 1. Horns enter on beat 1 of bar 2. Cello enters two beats before horns. Flute enters on the last beat of bar 2.
questions.explanation: Drums sit on beat 2. Horns are beat 5, so cello is beat 3. Flute takes the last beat of bar 2, which is beat 8.

questions.prompt: Using the clock rules, order the four entrances from earliest to latest.
questions.context: Each beat lasts 500 milliseconds, and 1 second equals 1000 milliseconds. Time 0 is the first count-in click. Piano enters after 3 beats. Violin enters at 1750 ms. Choir enters at 2 seconds. Harp enters half a beat before piano.
questions.explanation: Piano is at 1500 ms and harp half a beat (250 ms) earlier, at 1250 ms. Violin follows at 1750 ms, then choir at 2000 ms.

questions.prompt: Order these four entrances from earliest to latest by chaining the cues.
questions.context: The count-in ends on beat 4. Viola enters two beats after the count-in ends. Oboe enters one beat after viola. Triangle enters halfway between viola and oboe. Tuba enters two beats after oboe.
questions.explanation: Viola lands on beat 6 and oboe on beat 7. Triangle sits halfway at beat 6.5, and tuba comes two beats after oboe at beat 9.

questions.prompt: Which single change resolves the conflict between keys and bass?
questions.context: Beats are numbered continuously. Bass is locked to enter on beat 5 and cannot move. Keys must enter exactly one beat before bass, but the chart currently cues keys on beat 5 too.
questions.explanation: Bass is fixed at beat 5, so keys must take beat 4. Moving bass breaks the lock, and the other options miss the one-beat gap.

questions.prompt: At what time should the singer's cue move so the rules are satisfied?
questions.context: One beat lasts 600 ms, with time 0 at the end of the count-in. Guitar enters 3 beats after time 0. The singer must enter 2 beats after guitar, but is currently cued at 1500 ms.
questions.explanation: Guitar enters at 3 × 600 = 1800 ms. Two more beats add 1200 ms, so the singer belongs at 3000 ms.

questions.prompt: Which cello cue fixes the conflict in this three-beat-bar chart?
questions.context: Every bar has 3 beats. Flute enters on beat 1 of bar 3. Cello must enter on the final beat of the bar just before the flute entrance. The chart currently cues cello on beat 1 of bar 2.
questions.explanation: The bar before the flute entrance is bar 2, and its final beat is beat 3. Beat 1 of bar 3 would collide with the flute.

questions.prompt: Which beat should the trombone take to resolve the collision with the trumpet?
questions.context: Drums hit on beats 1, 2, 3 and 4. Trumpet enters two beats after the second drum hit. Trombone must enter half of a four-beat bar after the trumpet, but is currently cued on beat 4.
questions.explanation: The second drum hit is beat 2, so the trumpet enters on beat 4. Half of a four-beat bar is 2 beats, putting the trombone on beat 6.

title: Music Myth Checkpoint
description: Judge popular music claims as supported, partly true, or unsupported using supplied evidence, then spot the missing context that stops a broad claim from holding up.

sections.title: Judge the claim
sections.description: Use the evidence on each card.

questions.prompt: Judge the claim: 'Louder always means a better recording.' Which verdict fits the evidence below?
questions.context: Invented listening test, 20 listeners, one performance in two versions. Unmatched volume: 15 chose the louder version. Level-matched: 10 chose louder, 10 chose quieter. Supported = true in every case; partly true = true in some cases, not others; unsupported = contradicted.
questions.explanation: Loudness swayed preference when levels differed, but the preference split once levels were matched. 'Always' fails, yet the effect is not zero.

questions.prompt: Judge the claim: 'A faster tempo makes the pitch higher.' What does the supplied evidence show?
questions.context: Invented clips: Clip 1 plays a 440 Hz tone once per beat at 60 beats per minute. Clip 2 plays the same 440 Hz tone at 120 beats per minute. Tempo describes timing; frequency describes pitch.

options.label: Supported only above 100 beats per minute

questions.explanation: Both clips use 440 Hz, so pitch stayed the same while tempo doubled. Rhythm and pitch are separate properties.

questions.prompt: Match each claim to the verdict the supplied evidence supports.
questions.context: Quarter note = 1 beat; eighth note = half a beat. At 120 beats per minute a quarter note lasts 500 ms; at 60 it lasts 1000 ms. At 2 pulses per second each lasts 0.5 s; at 4 per second, 0.25 s. An invented 6/8 clip has six eighth subdivisions, accented at 1 and 4 as two groups of three.

left.label: Doubling pulses per second halves each pulse's length.
A quarter note always lasts exactly 500 ms.
6/8 has six subdivisions, so it is always felt as six equal beats.
At one tempo, an eighth note is half as long as a quarter note.

questions.explanation: Note lengths depend on tempo, so 'always 500 ms' fails. Six subdivisions are real, but the accents group them into two, so that claim is only partly true.

questions.prompt: Using the timing rules, rate each timing claim.
questions.context: 1 s = 1000 ms. Beats per minute = 60000 ÷ milliseconds per beat. A beat at 120 beats per minute lasts 500 ms. An eighth note is half a beat.

cells.label: A pulse every 250 ms gives four pulses each second.
A 0.6 s beat equals 60 beats per minute.
At 120 beats per minute, an eighth note lasts 250 ms.

questions.explanation: 1000 ÷ 250 = 4 pulses per second, and half of 500 ms is 250 ms. A 0.6 s beat is 60000 ÷ 600 = 100 beats per minute, not 60.

questions.prompt: Which missing detail most directly stops this broad claim from being supported?
questions.context: Invented case: Maple Street Choir made 30% fewer errors after trying a warm-up app. Claim: 'This app cuts errors for every choir.'

options.label: The color of the rehearsal room walls
Whether the choir also added extra rehearsals in that period

questions.explanation: If rehearsals increased at the same time, the app cannot be credited alone. One choir also cannot represent every choir.

questions.prompt: Which missing detail would you need before accepting the claim that fast tempos win more plays?
questions.context: Invented chart: all five most-played tracks on the Harbor Listen app run above 120 beats per minute. Claim: 'Fast tempo is what earns plays.'

options.label: The tempos of tracks that were not in the top five
The first names of the artists
The length of the app's name

questions.explanation: If many low-ranking tracks are also fast, tempo does not separate winners from others. A comparison group is needed.

questions.prompt: Match each claim to the limitation that most weakens it.
questions.context: Choose the one limitation that most obviously weakens each invented statement. A limitation can apply to more than one statement.

left.label: Only five people listened, and four chose Version B.
The audience clapped for 40 seconds after the new lighting.
Three of four listeners chose the shortest song.

questions.explanation: Groups of five or four are fragile evidence. Forty seconds means little without a prior show to compare against, and '90' could be beats per minute or something else.

questions.prompt: Order a fair test of the loudness claim. Steps that must come first should come first.
questions.context: Votes cannot be collected until levels are matched and the playback order is randomized. Totals are compared only after all votes are in. Matching and randomizing can happen in either order.

items.label: Match the playback level of both versions

questions.explanation: Matching level removes the loudness advantage, and randomizing removes order bias. Both must precede voting, and comparison comes last.

questions.context: Lantern Room (invented venue) rule: "Latecomers wait at the back door while a song is playing. Walk in only between songs. Staff can point you to open spots."

Wait at the back door until the song ends, then go in
Call to the staff across the room to ask mid-song
Squeeze past people quietly while the song plays

options.label: A 10-second video clip with no flash
A still photo with the flash on
A still photo with the flash off
A 30-second video, since that is the limit

8:55 pm, intact, but she already re-entered once tonight

Switch to a sparse, surprising texture and watch who reacts
Bring back a familiar anchor from earlier in the night

items.label: Jump suddenly to a high-energy track

questions.prompt: Order these three ideas from the one you would try first to the one you would try last.

items.label: Replay a track the room already loved

Let a guest pick the next track

title: Road Trip Playlist Treaty
description: Work together on one screen to fit mood blocks, tempos and pulse groupings into a three-hour drive, then seal a treaty that every invented passenger can accept.

sections.title: Fit the Stretch
sections.description: Time and pulse math for the drive.

sections.title: Read the Passengers
sections.description: Match moods and tempos to the cast.

sections.title: Seal the Treaty
sections.description: Resolve the final trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Together, work out how many Sing-along blocks are needed to fill the whole stretch.
questions.context: The drive is 3 hours. Every mood block lasts 20 minutes. The treaty already has 2 Calm blocks, 3 Upbeat blocks and 1 Surprise block.
questions.explanation: Three hours is 180 minutes, so there are 9 blocks of 20 minutes. Calm, Upbeat and Surprise use 6, leaving 3 for Sing-along.

questions.prompt: The driver's steady-energy cue pulses at 120 beats per minute. How long does each beat last?
questions.context: Use 1 minute = 60 seconds and 1 second = 1,000 milliseconds, so 1 minute = 60,000 ms. Beats are evenly spaced.
questions.explanation: Divide 60,000 ms by 120 beats to get 500 ms per beat. Evenly spaced beats make a steady pulse.

questions.prompt: The back seat wants a surprise bar of 7 beats grouped 3+2+2. On which beat does the third group begin?
questions.context: Count beats 1 to 7 in order. Each group starts right after the previous group ends, and the groups are 3 beats, then 2 beats, then 2 beats.
questions.explanation: The first group covers beats 1–3 and the second covers beats 4–5. The third group therefore starts on beat 6.

questions.prompt: Arrange the five blocks so every rule in the treaty is respected. Any valid order counts.
questions.context: Rules: Warm-up comes before every other block. Sing-along comes before Surprise. Quiet Lull comes before Finale. Finale is the last block.
questions.explanation: Warm-up must open and Finale must close. Sing-along must precede Surprise, while Quiet Lull can sit anywhere in between as long as it comes before Finale.

questions.prompt: Give each invented passenger the one mood block that fits what they said.
questions.context: Amara drives: "I need to stay alert, but I hate sudden jolts." Bao: "Make something unexpected appear." Lucía: "I want to join in on every chorus." Dalia: "I'm resting my eyes for this block."
questions.explanation: Each statement points to one block: alertness without jolts, the unexpected, joining choruses, and resting. The four blocks each serve exactly one person.

questions.prompt: Connect each tempo rule to every block whose tempo satisfies it.
questions.context: Block tempos: Steady Pulse 100 BPM, Surprise Mix 132 BPM, Sing-along 110 BPM, Quiet Lull 72 BPM. Rules include both endpoints.
questions.explanation: The 100–120 rule fits Steady Pulse and Sing-along. Only Quiet Lull is at most 80, and Surprise Mix and Sing-along fall within 105–135.

questions.prompt: The plan is 15 minutes too long. Which single cut makes the treaty fit and break no rule?
questions.context: Plan: Steady 60 min, Sing-along 50, Surprise 40, Quiet Lull 45, total 195 for a 180-minute drive. Rules: Surprise stays at 40, Steady stays at least 55, Quiet Lull stays at least 45, and no block drops under 30.
questions.explanation: Cutting Sing-along to 35 gives 60+35+40+45 = 180. Each other cut breaks a stated minimum or the fixed Surprise length.

questions.prompt: For the treaty card, match each block length to its equivalent in minutes.
questions.context: Use 1 minute = 60 seconds, 1 second = 1,000 ms and 1 hour = 60 minutes.
questions.explanation: 1,200,000 ms is 1,200 seconds, or 20 minutes. 1,800 seconds is 30 minutes, and half an hour is also 30 minutes.

dimensions.description: Whether you reach for sound that calms your mood down or stirs it up.
Whether you prefer a predictable beat or a rhythm that changes underfoot.

questions.prompt: On a rainy walk with headphones, which sound world would you pick for yourself?
questions.explanation: There is no right answer. Your pick shows whether you lean toward calming or stirring sound, and steady or changing rhythm.

options.label: Cozy: soft, slow and evenly pulsed
Bright: quick, lively and evenly pulsed
Dramatic: big swells and sudden rhythm changes
Hushed: quiet, drifting, with no clear beat

questions.prompt: A piece changes its beat grouping halfway through. How does that usually feel to you?
questions.explanation: This slider records your comfort with rhythmic change. Neither end is better; it is a conversation starter for your duet.

questions.prompt: Rank these four sound sketches for a late-night tidy-up, from most to least appealing.
questions.explanation: Your ranking gives each sketch a different mix of calming or stirring and steady or shifting, so order shows your leanings.

questions.prompt: Juno is walking in the rain. Which option does Juno pick?
questions.context: Juno is an invented listener. Rule 1: when it rains, Juno picks the option with the lowest tempo, measured in beats per minute (BPM).
questions.explanation: Rule 1 only compares tempo, and 60 BPM is the lowest of the four. Mood labels like bright or dramatic do not matter here.

questions.prompt: Match each of Juno's situations to the sound sketch Juno would choose.
questions.context: Invented rules. Tired: Juno picks the slowest steady option. Deadline: Juno picks the fastest steady option. Weekend cooking: Juno picks a changing pulse. Choices: Steady 70 BPM, steady 140 BPM, or changing pulse.
questions.explanation: Tired selects the slower steady sketch, the deadline the faster steady one, and cooking the only changing pulse.

questions.prompt: Convert each of Juno's playlist tempos into the time between beats.

questions.prompt: Without peeking, which rainy-walk sound world do you think your partner chose in the first round?

options.label: Cozy: soft, slow and evenly pulsed

title: Your Music Discovery Trail

questions.prompt: A friend says you would love their favorite band. What is your first move?
questions.explanation: This shows whether you reach for background or sound first, and whether you start with one release or a wide sampler. There is no right answer.
questions.context: You are free this evening and your phone is in hand. The band is new to you.

options.label: Press play on whatever song they name right now

Ask for one favorite album and play it start to finish
Save the name and decide later

questions.explanation: Your slider spot shows how much background you like before the first note. Neither end is better; they are different ways in.
questions.context: The page is invented. The story takes about five minutes to read, and the clip takes ten seconds.

questions.prompt: In an invented record shop, rank these four ways to spend a free hour from most to least appealing.
questions.explanation: Your order shows whether you lean toward reading context or sampling sound, and toward depth or breadth. Every item is a reasonable way to explore.
questions.context: The shop has staff-pick cards, ten preview stations, one full-album booth, and a clerk who loves local music history.

questions.prompt: A shared playlist of twelve unfamiliar songs from many places appears. How do you approach it?

questions.prompt: Match each discovery cue to the response you would most naturally have.
questions.explanation: Your matches reveal your habits across different triggers. Several cues can share one response, because habits often repeat.

title: Describe That Sound Out Loud
description: Practice plain-language sound vocabulary with three defined-word tasks, explore your own describing style in three preference tasks, then write two private descriptions of imagined sounds.

questions.prompt: An imagined drone is held for six seconds with no gaps. Which word fits, using these definitions?
questions.context: Definitions: sustained = continues without a break. Choppy = short bursts with silences between. Muffled = detail softened, as if covered. Pulsing = swells and fades again and again.
questions.explanation: A six-second sound with no gaps matches the supplied definition of sustained. Choppy needs silences, muffled concerns softened detail, and pulsing needs repeated swells.

questions.prompt: Match each tap pattern to the word that describes its spacing.
questions.context: Steady = every gap between neighboring taps is equal. Uneven = the gaps are not all equal. Patterns list tap times in seconds.
questions.explanation: Pattern X has 1-second gaps and Z has 0.5-second gaps, so both are steady. Pattern Y has gaps of 0.2, 1.3 and 0.1 seconds, so it is uneven.

questions.prompt: Which imagined sound counts as brief under the stated rule?
questions.context: Rule: brief means shorter than 0.5 seconds. Use 1 second = 1000 milliseconds to compare the options.
questions.explanation: 0.5 seconds equals 500 milliseconds, so only 300 ms is shorter. 650 ms, 0.9 s (900 ms) and 1.2 s (1200 ms) all run longer.

questions.prompt: Which opening line would you most likely write for a rainy-day bass hum?

options.label: A low, steady pressure you can feel in your chest.

The hum of a fridge behind a rain-streaked window.
A sleepy giant breathing beneath the rooftops.

questions.prompt: Rank these first moves for describing a sound, from most natural to least natural for you.

Tell a tiny story about who is making it

title: The Rhythm Switch
description: Listen to short synthetic pulse loops, find where the grouping switches between fours and threes, then match patterns and do simple timing arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Using the legend, how are these eight evenly spaced pulses grouped?
questions.context: Legend: a high tone (800 Hz) marks the first pulse of a group; a low tone (400 Hz) is any other pulse. Every pulse is 0.25 seconds apart. Press play, or read the transcript.
questions.transcript: Eight pulses, 0.25 s apart: high, low, low, low, high, low, low, low.
questions.explanation: High tones fall on pulses 1 and 5, so each group holds four pulses. That steady grouping is the baseline before any switch.

questions.prompt: Pulses are numbered 1 to 8. Which pulse starts the group of three after the group of four?
questions.context: Same legend: high tone starts a group, low tone continues it. Pulses are 0.25 seconds apart. This loop switches grouping once.
questions.transcript: Eight pulses, 0.25 s apart: high, low, low, low, high, low, low, high. Highs land on pulses 1, 5 and 8.
questions.explanation: The first high is pulse 1 and the next is pulse 5, making four. The following high is pulse 8, so pulses 5, 6 and 7 form the group of three.

questions.prompt: Before the final high tone, which order of group sizes do you hear?
questions.context: Same legend: a high tone starts a group; pulses are 0.25 seconds apart. The last high tone begins a new group that we do not hear finish.
questions.transcript: Eight pulses, 0.25 s apart: high, low, low, high, low, low, low, high. Highs land on pulses 1, 4 and 8.
questions.explanation: Highs on pulses 1, 4 and 8 give gaps of three and then four. This loop flips the opposite way from the previous one.

questions.prompt: Match each written pulse pattern to its grouping. H marks a group start; L is a continuing pulse.
questions.context: Each written pattern repeats without stopping, so count the pulses from one H to the next H.

left.label: H L L H L L
H L L L H L L L
H L H L H L

questions.explanation: Count pulses from each H to the next. A repeating H L L L is also groups of four, even though it is shorter on the page.

questions.prompt: For each loop, choose the grouping that fits where the strong pulses fall.
questions.context: Pulse counts start at 1. Strong pulses mark the start of each group, and the groups fill the whole loop.
questions.explanation: Subtract neighboring strong-pulse positions to get each group size. Gaps of 3 and 3, 4 and 4, or 2, 2 and 2 give the answers.

questions.prompt: Strong pulses fall on counts 1, 4, 7, 11 and 14. Which strong pulse begins the odd-length group?
questions.context: Each strong pulse starts a group that lasts until the next strong pulse. Three of the four complete groups here share one length.
questions.explanation: The gaps are 3, 3, 4 and 3. Only the group from count 7 to count 10 has four pulses, so that is where the feel stretches.

questions.prompt: A pulse sounds every 500 ms. How many pulses begin during a 3-second stretch, counting the first at time zero but not the one at 3 s?
questions.context: Use 1 second = 1000 milliseconds. The first pulse sounds at 0 ms.
questions.explanation: 3 seconds is 3000 ms, and 3000 divided by 500 is 6. Pulses start at 0, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500 ms.

questions.prompt: Order these loops from shortest to longest total duration (pulses times spacing).
questions.context: Use 1 second = 1000 ms. Total duration = number of pulses multiplied by the spacing between pulses.
questions.explanation: Loop B lasts 1000 ms, C 1050 ms, A 1200 ms and D 1500 ms. Converting everything to milliseconds makes the comparison direct.

title: Loop Layer Lab
description: Listen to short invented tone loops, name which layer just joined, then read cue sheets to order layers by entrance. Scored out of 8.

questions.prompt: A steady loop plays, then something new joins at the third tick. Which layer arrived?
questions.context: Legend: rhythm layer = very short 0.08 s ticks near 800 Hz. Bass layer = long 0.4 s tones near 200–250 Hz. Melody layer = medium 0.2 s tones between 500 and 650 Hz. Ticks run the whole time.
questions.explanation: The ticks were present from the start. Long low tones near 220 Hz match the bass legend, so bass is the newcomer.
questions.transcript: Four short 800 Hz ticks, one every half second. From the third tick on, two long 220 Hz tones, each 0.4 seconds, play along with the ticks.

questions.prompt: Low tones repeat, then a new layer enters on the last one. Which layer is the newcomer?
questions.context: Legend: rhythm = 0.08 s ticks near 800 Hz. Bass = long 0.4 s tones near 200–250 Hz. Melody = 0.2 s tones between 500 and 650 Hz. Bass tones are heard from the start of the clip.
questions.explanation: Bass was already repeating. The two medium, shorter tones at 520 and 640 Hz fit the melody legend, and the pitch change makes them a tune.
questions.transcript: Three long 220 Hz tones, 0.8 seconds apart. During the third one, a 520 Hz tone and then a 640 Hz tone, each 0.2 seconds, join above it.

questions.prompt: A melody changes pitch partway through. Which layer is actually new in this clip?
questions.context: Legend: rhythm = 0.08 s ticks near 800 Hz. Bass = long 0.4 s tones near 200–250 Hz. Melody = 0.2 s tones between 500 and 650 Hz. A layer is new only if it was silent earlier in the clip.
questions.explanation: The melody sounds from the start, so its pitch change is not a new layer. The 800 Hz ticks first appear at 0.8 seconds, so rhythm is new.
questions.transcript: Medium tones at 560, 640, 560 and 640 Hz play at 0, 0.4, 0.8 and 1.2 seconds. From 0.8 seconds, three short 800 Hz ticks, 0.2 seconds apart, are added.

questions.prompt: Ticks and bass are already looping. One lone extra tone appears near the end. Which layer is it?
questions.context: Legend: rhythm = 0.08 s ticks near 800 Hz. Bass = long 0.4 s tones near 200–250 Hz. Melody = 0.2 s tones between 500 and 650 Hz. Match the new tone by its length and pitch.
questions.explanation: Ticks and bass were both present from the start. The single 0.2 s tone at 580 Hz sits in the melody range, so melody is entering.
questions.transcript: Five short 800 Hz ticks, 0.4 seconds apart. Two long 230 Hz tones at 0 and 0.8 seconds. At 1.2 seconds a single 0.2 second tone at 580 Hz is added.

questions.prompt: Use the legend to label each tone profile from a producer's note with its layer.
questions.context: Legend: rhythm = very short ticks of about 0.08 s near 800 Hz. Bass = long 0.4 s tones near 200–250 Hz. Melody = 0.2 s tones from 500 to 650 Hz. Remember 1 s = 1,000 ms.
questions.explanation: Match by length and pitch. 80 ms equals 0.08 s, so it is a tick. 400 ms equals 0.4 s, which is long. Mid-range 200 ms tones are melody.

questions.prompt: A loop has four beats per bar at 0.5 seconds per beat. At what second does bar five begin?
questions.context: Bar one starts at 0 s. Every bar lasts the same time, and the tempo never changes.
questions.explanation: Each bar lasts 4 × 0.5 = 2 seconds. Four full bars take 8 seconds, so bar five starts at the 8 second mark.

questions.prompt: Put these invented layers in the order they first enter the loop, earliest first.
questions.context: Drums start the track. Bass enters one bar after the drums. Pad enters two bars after the bass. Lead enters one bar after the pad.
questions.explanation: Each clue chains from the previous layer: drums, then bass, then pad, then lead. Only that one order satisfies every entrance gap.

questions.prompt: A mix log lists entrance times in mixed units. Order the layers from earliest to latest entrance.
questions.context: Use 1 s = 1,000 ms. Lead enters at 2,000 ms. Bass enters at 0.5 s. Chords enter at 1.75 s. Shaker enters at 1,250 ms.
questions.explanation: Converted to seconds: bass 0.5, shaker 1.25, chords 1.75, lead 2.0. Sorting those values gives the entrance order.

title: Mood Loops: Pick Your Pulse

sections.title: Pick a Loop
sections.description: Listen to two tone loops and choose one.

dimensions.description: Whether you lean toward few, widely spaced sounds or many sounds packed close together.

questions.prompt: Play both loops. Which one would you rather keep running in the background?

Loop B: four high, bright blips

questions.prompt: Now the traits are mixed. Which loop would you rather loop on repeat?

Loop B: five low soft notes in a row

questions.prompt: Last pair. Which loop feels more like your kind of background sound?

questions.transcript: Loop A: two long, soft 240 Hz sine notes, 0.4 seconds each, 0.8 seconds apart. Loop B: six very short 900 Hz triangle ticks, 0.08 seconds each, every 0.1 seconds.

options.label: Loop A: two long, soft, low notes
Loop B: six rapid, high ticks

questions.explanation: Both traits now move together, giving the clearest contrast of the four pairs. Your choice nudges both preference scales at once.

questions.prompt: You have a two-hour work session. Which kind of loop would you keep playing?

options.label: A slow, spacious loop with soft low notes
A slow, spacious loop with a few bright accents

A tight, busy loop with a driving, bright feel

questions.explanation: Work music is personal: some people want room to think, others want a steady busy texture. All four choices are valid preferences.

questions.prompt: Rank these loop styles for a morning commute, from the one you would most like to hear to the least.

items.label: Wide-open slow loop with low, soft notes
Sparse loop with bright, sharp blips
Fast, packed loop with high, bright ticks

questions.explanation: Ranking shows your whole order of taste, not just one pick. Items you place higher count more toward your two preference scales.

questions.prompt: Thinking of the loops you picked, how much energy do you want them to carry?
questions.explanation: This slider adds directly to your calm-to-charged preference scale. Neither end is better.

questions.prompt: And how much texture should your ideal loop have: open air or layered fullness?
questions.explanation: This slider adds directly to your spacious-to-dense preference scale, reflecting how much sound you like filling the room.

title: The Unfinished Sign-Off
description: Follow an original three-note tune from a broadcast fragment to a music box—and an unexpected reply. Listen to two short sketches, uncover the source and shape the final arrangement.

questions.prompt: What musical fingerprint can you recognize when this tune returns?
questions.context: Original fictional scene. In “The Unfinished Sign-Off,” the opening broadcast uses only the first two notes of a tune. The complete three-note theme below is a listener reference, not a claim that Ren has already found its ending. Play this soft synthetic sketch or read its full text equivalent. Which observable fingerprint will let you recognize the theme when it returns?
questions.explanation: Each phrase begins on 330 Hz, rises to 440 Hz, then falls to 392 Hz, still above the starting pitch. The last note lasts longer than either of the first two. The same phrase repeats, giving the story a recognizable musical fingerprint.

options.label: Three notes descending, with the first held longest.
Three equal notes, with the middle held longest.
A rise, then a smaller fall, with the last note held longer.
A rise that continues upward on the held last note.

questions.transcript: Two identical, soft three-note phrases, with no accompaniment or voice. Each phrase starts on a middle note, rises to a higher note, then falls partway back: the last note is below the second but above the first. The last note is held longer than either of the first two. Short quiet gaps separate the notes; a longer silent gap separates the two phrases. Both phrases use the same rounded synthetic sine tone.

questions.prompt: Which arrangement lets the listener notice the fragment hiding behind Ren’s announcement?
questions.context: Original fictional scene. Story score: Ren is reading a station sign-off. The music under the words uses the tune’s first two notes, then leaves its final note missing. The production brief requires the announcement to remain clear and that missing ending to be audible in a gap after the words. This is a written cue plan; the preview does not synthesize speech.
questions.explanation: The quiet fragment preserves the speech, and the exposed gap makes its missing final note noticeable. A complete repeat removes the very absence the scene needs; replacing or sustaining the music loses the recognizable fragment.

options.label: Repeat the complete tune loudly throughout the announcement.
Keep the fragment quiet under the words, then leave space where its final note would be.
Remove the fragment and fill every speech gap with a different tune.
Hold one continuous note across the announcement and its ending.

questions.prompt: When the second version arrives, what has changed and what has stayed?
questions.context: Original fictional scene. Ren follows the tune into the station’s storage room. This preview compares two arrangements of that same original phrase. Listen to both or read the complete equivalent. The lower sustained layer belongs only to the first version.
questions.explanation: The pitches, note lengths and spacing of the three-note phrase stay the same. First it sits above a low sine tone; later it plays alone in triangle tones. That preserves recognition while stripping away the surrounding layer.

options.label: The second phrase reverses its note order and keeps the lower layer.
The note order stays, but the second phrase is alone and has a different tone colour.
The second phrase keeps only the first two notes and omits the long ending.
The second phrase is the same sound with an added low layer.

questions.transcript: First version: a quiet, steady low tone accompanies a higher three-note phrase. The phrase rises, then falls partway back; its last note is held longest. The low tone continues briefly after that phrase ends, and then all sound stops. After a silent gap, the identical phrase returns alone: same note order, note lengths and spacing, but a different synthetic tone colour (triangle instead of sine). No low accompaniment plays under the second phrase. No speech or physical object sounds are simulated.

questions.prompt: What does Ren’s stop-and-restart test support about the tune’s source?
questions.context: Original fictional scene. The station’s playback deck is muted. A separate live microphone in the storage room is still audible. With the small box lid open, that microphone carries the complete phrase. Ren closes the lid mid-phrase: the tune stops. Reopening the lid brings the phrase back from its beginning. No other device or control changes during this test.
questions.explanation: The repeated connection between the lid action and the live tune, while station playback is muted, supports the box as a source in this test. It does not identify every other sound in the story, predict all later arrangements, or make a claim about a supernatural cause.

options.label: Every musical sound heard anywhere in the story must come from the box.
The station playback deck is the only source heard during this test.
The box is contributing the tune to the live room microphone during the test.
The tune’s last note will always be absent in every later arrangement.

questions.prompt: Classify these rehearsal sketches by what they preserve or change in the theme.
questions.context: Original fictional score. Ren’s signature has three notes: up, then partway down, with its last note held longest. In this arrangement brief, moving the entire melody higher or lower and changing its backing are allowed; removing the ending or changing that relative contour changes what the listener has to recognize. The sketches below are written descriptions, not extra audio clips.
questions.explanation: Moving all notes together preserves the relative shape and rhythm: a whole-theme variation, not an exact replay of the same pitches. The second sketch omits the ending. The third changes the final pitch’s relation to the start. Backing and register changes are therefore different from losing or rewriting part of this particular theme.

left.label: Every melody note moves lower by the same amount; the contour and rhythm stay, with a low backing layer added.
The first two notes return, followed by silence where the held ending would be.
Three notes remain, but the last drops below the starting note instead of landing between the first two.

right.label: Complete theme in a new register

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the recording session from the envelope, box and reel states.
questions.context: Original fictional scene. Four fragments come from the same session. The only box key starts in one sealed envelope, which is opened once and never resealed. One blank reel becomes the NEW SIGN-OFF recording; it is never erased, replaced or relabelled. The recorder does not play an unrecorded reel. Use the state changes in the cards, not their scrambled list order.
questions.explanation: The sealed key envelope must precede its opened state beside the open box. The blank reel precedes the completed recording, and only that recorded reel can supply the final playback. These changing objects force d → b → c → a, so the arrangement’s completion becomes something the story actually records before it uses it.

items.label: Box lid closed; the deck plays the reel marked NEW SIGN-OFF.
Envelope open, key in the box lock, lid raised; the reel in the recorder is blank.
The recorder has just finished; its reel now bears NEW SIGN-OFF, and the box remains open.
Ren finds the sealed key envelope while the old unfinished sign-off is playing.

questions.prompt: The ending must let us hear a reply, not just a thickened version of the tune. Which score does that?
questions.context: Original fictional scene. Final scene: with the box now closed, Ren plays the recorded phrase. In the original story, a second phrase then sounds from the empty storage room. Keep the first phrase recognizable and make the second entrance separately noticeable. Neither cue may cover the other.
questions.explanation: A completed phrase, silence and a separate answer make two events available to the listener. Simultaneous or overlapping versions can instead read as one layered arrangement. The score supports this particular reply structure without claiming everyone will find it frightening.

options.label: Start both versions together at the same pitch and pace.
Play the recording, leave a clear quiet gap, then let the room’s phrase answer alone.
Keep a continuous low note and omit both three-note phrases.
Play the second phrase only beneath the longest note of the first.

questions.prompt: Which explanation of the late reply can Ren rule out from this two-track record?
questions.context: Original fictional scene. The final recording keeps two working inputs separate: the station deck’s direct output and the live storage-room microphone. Neither track is muted, edited or overdubbed. The station track records its complete sign-off, then stays silent. After that, a matching phrase appears on the room-microphone track while the station track remains silent. No late camera view identifies the room’s sound source.
questions.explanation: If the same deck had replayed through its direct output, that working, unmuted track would also contain the reply. It does not. The room track establishes that sound reached its microphone, but does not distinguish a spare player, the box or another live source. The ending leaves an actual source question open instead of merely repeating a mysterious caption.

options.label: A second player somewhere in the room supplied the reply.
The music box began playing again through an unseen action.
The same station deck played the reply through its recorded direct output.
Another live source in the room produced a matching phrase.

questions.explanation: An added quiet offbeat does not replace the two marked strong beats or the underlying three-pulse groups.

options.label: Yes, the main accents now repeat in pairs
No; the strong-soft-soft main pulses remain, with an added quiet offbeat
The offbeat is the only strong beat

questions.transcript: Main pulses at the same even pace as before: STRONG, soft, soft, STRONG, soft, soft. An extra very quiet tap occurs halfway between the third main pulse and the fourth. The regular footsteps continue without speeding up.

questions.prompt: The ghost leaves one weak step silent. What evidence still lets the dancer find the next turn?
questions.context: Original score note: STRONG, soft, rest; STRONG, soft, soft. The rest occupies one pulse slot. The two STRONG marks stay in their usual places.
questions.explanation: A rest can occupy a pulse position; the returning strong beat still starts the next three-pulse group.

options.label: The next strong mark arrives after the same three pulse slots
The soft step becomes the only strong one

questions.prompt: Match each rehearsal difficulty to the adjustment that preserves the intended cue.
questions.context: These are three separate problems in the original rehearsal. Keep the composed accent pattern unless the card specifically asks to follow the changed exit cue.
questions.explanation: The fixes separate three issues: added decoration does not accelerate the main pulse, a rest keeps its allotted time, and a genuinely changed accent cycle asks for a new movement grouping.

left.label: The extra quiet tap makes the dancer speed up, although the main footsteps have not changed
The dancer skips a silent weak slot and reaches the next big turn early
At the paired exit cue, the dancer keeps taking two small steps between big turns

right.label: Hold the silent pulse position instead of deleting its time
Use one small step between big turns for the new cue
Keep the original even footsteps and let the quieter tap fall between them

questions.prompt: The exit cue sounds unlike the opening. What changed in the main accent cycle?
questions.context: The exit uses the same pulse spacing and number of main pulses as the opening. Compare where its accents return.
questions.explanation: The exit has three strong-soft pairs; its strong beats recur more often than in the opening.

options.label: The strong pulse now returns after one soft pulse
The strong pulse still returns after two soft pulses

questions.transcript: Six evenly spaced pulses: STRONG, soft, STRONG, soft, STRONG, soft. No extra in-between tap.

questions.prompt: Arrange three rehearsal cards from the longest gap between big turns to the shortest.
questions.context: All three original cues keep exactly the same pulse speed. A big turn begins on each STRONG; each soft pulse is a small step. Compare the recurring accent cycle, rather than the length of a recording.
questions.explanation: At one shared pulse speed, three soft steps separate the broad turns on the first card in this order, then two, then one. This compares the written accent cycles; it does not infer a written time-signature denominator.

questions.prompt: How would you end this tiny haunted dance?
questions.context: The composed cue has reached the door in strong-soft pairs. Choose an artistic finish for an imaginary performance. The quiz records a choice; it does not create or change the soundtrack.
questions.explanation: Each finish changes the dramatic emphasis: interruption, a deliberate farewell, or a lingering presence. This is an ungraded artistic choice, with no best ending or personality claim.

options.label: Let the final pair stop abruptly, leaving the dancer facing the closed door
Finish with one last broad turn, then hold the empty doorway in silence
Bring back the quiet in-between tap once after the dancer has left
